title: Mastery Challenge: Earth, Weather & Climate
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Earth, Weather & Climate Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Ten questions, one from each chapter: rocks, plates, landscapes, deep time, the air, weather, storms, past climates, climate change and the choices it raises. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Earth, Weather & Climate Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions from across the tree, from a grain of quartz to the forecast on your phone. Level 1 split the planet into four spheres; now see how far that picture reaches. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Earth, Weather & Climate: mastered
learned: How rock, air, water and life link into one system, from a cooling lava flow to a changing climate.
Why plates, rivers and deep time build and wear down land, and how geologists date the rocks.
How rising air makes clouds and storms, and why carbon dioxide has long set Earth's temperature.
How scientists know recent warming is ours, and how people weigh the choices for responding.

questions.prompt: Rocks and Minerals: match each igneous rock with how it formed.

pairs.right: Erupts and cools fast at the surface

questions.explanation: Granite cools slowly, deep underground, basalt erupts and cools fast at the surface, and obsidian is lava chilled so fast it becomes natural volcanic glass.

questions.prompt: Plates and Quakes: the ground beside a locked fault, fences and all, slowly bends over many years, too gently to see without precise instruments. What is happening?

options.label: The fence posts are slowly rotting and leaning over
options.rationale: The ground itself is bending, not the posts.

options.label: Strain is building in the rock, ready to snap back in a quake
The fault is creeping smoothly, so no big quake can ever come
options.rationale: A locked fault stores strain; it doesn't release it.

options.label: Magma is rising underneath and lifting the ground
options.rationale: This is a transform fault, not a volcano.

questions.explanation: Moving plates bend the rock beside a locked fault and it stores strain like a bent ruler. When the fault slips, the rock snaps back: an earthquake.

questions.prompt: Shaping the Land: a river floods across its floodplain. Why does it leave levees and fertile silt behind?

options.label: Floodwater dissolves the bedrock into new soil
options.rationale: The silt is carried in, not dissolved in place.

options.label: The flood cuts a deeper V-shaped valley
options.rationale: Cutting down is erosion; this is deposition.

options.label: Wind blows dust onto the wet ground
options.rationale: The river delivers this load, not the wind.

options.label: Spreading out slows the water, so it drops its load

questions.explanation: Slow water drops what it can no longer carry: coarse grains build levees by the channel, and finer silt settles farther out.

questions.prompt: Deep Time: a trilobite has no usable radioactive clock. How can geologists still put an age on it?

options.label: Count the rings in its shell like a tree
options.rationale: Shells don't record years that way.

options.label: Assume every fossil is about the same age
options.rationale: Fossils span hundreds of millions of years.

options.label: Date volcanic ash layers above and below it
Measure how deep it is buried in meters
options.rationale: Depth gives order, not years.

questions.explanation: Ash crystals start their clocks when they form. Dating ash below and above the fossils pins them between the two ages.

questions.prompt: The Atmosphere: extra greenhouse gas cuts the heat escaping to space. Why doesn't Earth then heat up forever?

options.label: A warmer surface sheds more heat until the budget balances
The Sun automatically dims a little to make up for the change
options.rationale: The brake is on Earth's side, not the Sun's.

options.label: Greenhouse gases break down as soon as the air warms
options.rationale: They don't vanish when it warms.

options.label: Oceans absorb all extra heat with no warming at all
options.rationale: The surface still warms to a new balance.

questions.explanation: As the surface warms, the heat it radiates rises quickly, so Earth settles at a new, higher temperature where energy in matches energy out.

questions.prompt: How Weather Works: wind pushes moist air up a mountainside, and a cloud forms. Why?

options.label: The mountain's cold rock chills the air it touches
options.rationale: The air cools by expanding, not by touch.

options.label: It expands, cools to its dew point, and its vapor condenses
It soaks up extra water vapor from the thin, cold air above
options.rationale: The vapor was already in the air.

options.label: Higher air is closer to the Sun, which dries it out
options.rationale: Distance from the Sun isn't the cause.

questions.explanation: Rising air meets lower pressure, spreads out and cools. Cooled to its dew point, its water vapor condenses into cloud droplets.

questions.prompt: Storms: a slow, wide Category 1 hurricane is heading inland. Why can it still be very dangerous?

options.label: A low category means it is about to strengthen quickly
options.rationale: Category says nothing about future strength.

options.label: Every Category 1 storm is certain to spawn tornadoes far inland
options.rationale: Tornadoes are possible in any category, not certain.

options.label: Its winds are far stronger than its category shows
options.rationale: The number does reflect its wind.

options.label: Category rates only wind; slow, wide storms drop the most rain

questions.explanation: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates only maximum sustained wind. Rain depends on a storm's speed and size, so slow, large storms of any category can flood.

questions.prompt: Climates Past and Present: volcanoes pump extra carbon dioxide into the air for ages. How does rock weathering ease the warming?

options.label: Weathered rock reflects more sunlight, just like snow
options.rationale: The effect runs through carbon, not reflection.

options.label: Cooler weather slows weathering, so carbon stays in the air
options.rationale: It's the other way: warmth speeds weathering.

options.label: Warmth brings more rain, so more carbon washes to the sea floor
Weathering releases oxygen that breaks down the extra carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Carbon is carried to the ocean, not destroyed.

questions.explanation: Carbonic acid in rain dissolves rock, and the carbon ends up locked in limestone. Warmth speeds this up, so the warming eases.

questions.prompt: Climate Change: the Sun's energy shows no upward trend since 1978, and the stratosphere is cooling while the surface warms. Which explanation fits both?

options.label: The Sun growing slowly brighter each year
options.rationale: A brighter Sun would warm every layer.

options.label: Greenhouse gases trapping more heat down low
Big eruptions heating the air year after year
options.rationale: Eruptions cool the planet for a few years.

options.label: Satellites measuring the Sun's output wrongly
options.rationale: The measurements show no upward trend.

questions.explanation: A brighter Sun would warm all layers. Warming below with cooling above is the pattern expected when gases trap heat down low.

questions.prompt: Forecasts, Hazards and Choices: which pair best sums up the main arguments for and against carbon pricing?

options.label: For: no CO2 while running. Against: long-lived waste
options.rationale: Those points are about nuclear power.

options.label: For: it ends all emissions at once. Against: it's illegal
options.rationale: Neither is the argument either side makes.

options.label: For: it's cost-effective. Against: it weighs more on lower-income homes
For: it cools the planet very quickly. Against: it can harm the ozone layer
options.rationale: Those points are about solar geoengineering.

questions.explanation: Supporters call carbon pricing a cost-effective way to cut emissions; critics say higher energy costs hit lower-income households harder.
